posts.content_md:
I have just found that the bright yellow rinse water you get after using the thermal hardening DCG method can be "cured" in under a minute by just adding a pinch of vitamin C. powder. The water appears to go completely colorless.

Now that begs the question could vitamin C solution be used as an alternative to the Kodak fix hardener system . Last November here we had a a discussion (see below) on doing away with the Kodak fix hardener as I indicated that it was mainly the reducing agent metabisulfite in the Kodak product that was completing the reduction of CrV from exposed dichromate bright fringes and that it would be best if one could make up a simple solution of metabisulfite instead. Now it looks as though straight healthy ubiquitous ascorbic acid powder would do the job instead.

[http://www.holographyforum.org/phpBB2/v ... sc&start=0](http://www.holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=4127&postdays=0&postorder=asc&start=0)

and also on John Pecora’s thread next to it on RED SHIFTING DCG.

jeff.

Well, when I heard this I ran right to my refrigerator. We make a lot of iced tea and I use ReaLemon lemon juice concentrate. I figure lemon juice concentrat has vitamin C if it has not been left open to air too long.

[http://asianwok.com/markets/productDeta ... s&nextID=1](http://asianwok.com/markets/productDetail.asp?productID=10452&categoryID=1230&categoryName=Juice+Ingredients&nextID=1)

So what are the odds...???...!!!

Look at the ingredients.

Ingredients 

Lemon juice from concentrate(water, concentrated lemon juice), sodium bisulfite(preservative), sodium benzoate (preservative) and lemon oil. 

Sodium Bisulfite is number two on the list. And although the per serving does not state any Vitamin C and I bet it has some. But I am not sure of the effects Sodium Benzonate would have. Jeff?

So I took a plate that still had some yellow to it, made up a concentration of 10% lemon concentrate with water and it took away the yellow. I don't believe either of the sodiums will take away the yellow so there has to be something else in lemon juice that does, possible vitamin C?

Unfortunately I could not try the Lemon concentrate by itself instead of the Kodak Fixer but I will on my next session. Boy I would love to be able to switch to ReaLemon instead of Kodak Rapid Fixer.

Now, this brings up an interesting question. Would the Vitamin C work in bleaching Silver Halide holograms?

posts.author: Ron Michael
posts.content_md:
Paints, alodine, turns out I've got chromates laying around and I've been reading about the problem with hexavalent chromium (a carcinogen ) in the ground water supply and also about using in-situ remediation efforts instead of letting this stuff loose in my environment. One method I researched looks pretty good and easy enough for us in holography is to reduce the Cr(VI) to trivalent chromium with hydrogen sulfite in a low ph solution. The dichromate bleach solution generally is around ph 2.4 as given by mix formula. To Remediate the dichromate bleach solution or any chromate/dichromate solution as long as the ph is below 4 and best below 3 is to add sodium metasulfite (metabisulfite Na2S2O5 is available at photography formulary etc) until the solution is bright green and then extra to be sure or you can work out the formula if you happen to know the amount of chromates in solution you have. As Jeff mentioned, Na2S2O5 in water hydrolysis forms Sodium hydrogen sulfite (bisulfite) NaHSO3. The insoluble relative non-toxic chromium III hydroxide settles out as precipitate So you can then pour off the solution and find a chemical dump etc for the precipitate. If you have a ph meter then by all means add some sodium bisulfate or sulfuric acid before hand to adjust the ph to below 3 to ensure reduction. My understanding is that most but sometimes not all Cr(VI) will be reduced to Cr(III) using the acid reduction with sulfites method. Other methods of reducing using Fe(II) or Mn(II) were discussed as a remediation effort. Here is a reference to chromium chemistry including using zinc to reduce Cr(VI) to Cr(III) : 

[http://www.chemguide.co.uk/inorganic/tr ... omium.html](http://www.chemguide.co.uk/inorganic/transition/chromium.html)

Personally, I like the SM-6 developer because it's low toxic, I'm going to give Phillips Safe Solvent Bleach a try and reduce my chromium risk and avoid "chrom holes" etc
